en: Sutta Nipāta 3.11 Nālakasutta:
When the throngs of the Thirty-three gods had departed, overcome with joy,
While on his midday rest, the seer Asita saw Sakka the Lord of Gods and the gods in their pure garments, holding cloths and praising him exceedingly.
Having seen the gods there with joyful minds and uplifted spirits,
he fixed his attention and spoke this:
“Why is the assembly of gods so exceedingly beautiful?
"Taking up your garments, why do you rejoice?
Even when there was a conflict with the Asuras,
it was the Suras who were victorious and the Asuras who were defeated."
Even then, such was the hair-raising leader;
what wonder was it that the gods were so delighted?
They shouted, sang, and played musical instruments.
They snap their arms and dance about;
I ask you, O dwellers on the summit of Mount Meru,
quickly dispel my doubt, O Noble Ones!
Thus the Bodhisatta, the incomparable jewel among beings,
was born for the sake of the welfare and happiness of the world of men,
in the village of the Śākyas, in the region of Lumbinī.
Therefore we are exceedingly joyful and of beautiful form.
He is the supreme among all beings, the foremost person,
the bull among men, the most excellent of all creatures.
"The wheel shall turn in the forest called Isipatana,
like the roar of a powerful lion that overcomes other beasts.
Hearing that sound, he hurriedly approached.
Then he entered the palace of Śuddhodana;
having sat down there, he said this to the Śākyas:
"Where is the prince? I, too, wish to see him."
Then the prince, like well-refined gold blazing in the mouth of a furnace,
shone with splendor, possessed of a peerless complexion.
The Sakyans gave a son to Asita by name.
Having seen the prince, blazing like a crest of fire,
pure and moving through the sky like the preeminent star;
Seeing the sun blazing, released from the clouds of autumn,
he was born of joy and attained vast rapture.
And [he saw] the thousand-spoked wheel with its many branches...
The gods held a parasol in the sky;
golden-handled yak-tail whisks were waved about,
yet neither the holders of the whisks nor the holders of the parasol were seen.
Seeing him, the matted-hair ascetic, the seer named Kaṇhasiri,
[beheld him] like a golden coin upon a pale woolen cloth,
with a white parasol being held over his head.
With an uplifted mind and joyful heart, he accepted it.
Having accepted it from the bull of the Sakyas, he,
a seeker of knowledge who had mastered the science of marks and mantras, [reflected].
With a serene mind, he uttered these words:
“The unsurpassed one among the best of bipeds.
Then, recollecting his own departure,
Unpleasantly, he shed tears;
seeing him weeping, the Sakyans said to the seer,
"If no misfortune shall befall the princes."
Having seen him, the Sakyan said to the seer at daybreak:
"I do not recall any harm to the prince;
nor will there be any obstacle for him."
Do not be conceited regarding this insignificant thing.
This prince shall touch the pinnacle of perfect enlightenment;
he, possessing supreme and purified vision, shall set in motion the Wheel of Dhamma.
This one who is compassionate for the welfare of many people will cause this holy life to spread;
and not much of my lifespan remains here.
"Yet death will come upon me in the meantime;
thus I shall not hear the Dhamma of the Peerless One.
Therefore I am distressed, fallen into calamity, and beset by misfortune."
Having thus generated great joy among the Sakyans,
he departed from the inner palace as one living the holy life;
out of compassion for his own nephew, he himself—
He incited [him] to the Dhamma, which is difficult to master:
"When you hear from another the cry 'Buddha,' one who has attained full enlightenment reveals the path of the Dhamma."
"Having gone there, questioning him at the proper time,
lead the holy life under that Blessed One.
Thus instructed by that benevolent and equanimous one,
In the future, Nālaka— possessing a vast accumulation of merit and guarding his sense faculties—
will dwell as an attendant to the Conqueror, who perceives the supreme purity.
Having heard the report concerning the wheel-turning of the Supreme Victor,
and having gone and seen the bull among seers, he was filled with faith;
he questioned the most excellent sage, the preeminent one in monasticism.
“When the teaching of the one named Asita has arrived.
The introductory verses are concluded.
“This word is understood.”
Of one who has transcended existence as it truly is;
that very thing, O Gotama, I ask you,
you who have gone to the further shore of all phenomena.
To me who has gone forth into homelessness and desires to practice the life of a mendicant,
O Sage, answer what I have asked.
“Moneyya is the supreme state.
“I shall explain moneyya to you,” [said the Blessed One].
It is difficult to do, hard to accomplish;
come now, I shall explain it to you—
be firm and steady.
One should treat with equanimity both reviling and praising in the village,
and guard against malice of mind.
Let the holy one wander without arrogance.
High and low sounds issue forth from the forest like crests of flame.
Women entice the sage;
let them not entice you.
One who abstains from sexual intercourse—
Having abandoned both higher and lower sensual pleasures,
he is unopposed and unattached toward living beings, whether moving or stationary.
As I am, so are these; as these are, so am I. Having made oneself the analogy, [one should not kill nor cause others to kill].
One should neither kill nor cause to be killed.
Having abandoned desire and greed—
that wherein the ordinary person is attached.
One with vision should practice thus;
one may cross over this hell.
With a slender belly and moderate food intake,
One who has few desires and is not greedy is always free from craving through the absence of longing;
being without desire, he is extinguished.
Having wandered for alms,
he should retire to the edge of the forest,
established at the foot of a tree.
The Sage, having taken his seat,
intent on meditation, wise,
may find delight in the forest edge.
One should meditate at the foot of a tree,
gladdening one's own self;
then, when the night has passed,
One should approach the edge of a village;
one should not rejoice in being invited,
nor in the bringing of offerings from the village.
The sage, having entered a village,
should not wander hastily among the families;
he should go for alms with his conversation cut off.
One should not utter speech that is discordant,
thinking, "I have gained this which is good," or "I have not gained what is wholesome."
Such a one, by both means,
returns like a bird to its tree;
wandering with alms-bowl in hand, he goes about.
Though not deaf, one may be considered deaf;
one should not despise a small gift,
nor should one disregard the giver.
For the path proclaimed by the Recluse is indeed manifold;
they do not go to the further shore by doubling it.
This is not understood as a single quality alone:
that in which there is no wavering,
in the case of a bhikkhu whose stream is cut.
For one who has abandoned what should be done and what should not be done, no fever exists.
I shall teach you that state of sagehood.
One should be like one carrying a burden;
having touched the palate with the tongue,
one should be restrained in the stomach.
One should be undaunted in mind and not harbor excessive thoughts;
free from the stench of raw flesh and unattached.
Devoted to the holy life,
one should train in eating at a single sitting and in attending upon ascetics.
Solitude is declared to be the sage’s way;
if you shall delight in solitude alone,
then you will illuminate the ten directions.
Having heard the proclamation of the wise,
those who meditate and have abandoned sensual desires,
one should then cultivate a sense of shame and faith.
My follower should do even more.
Discern that [destruction] through rivers,
and in ravines and fissures.
Small pools flow with a murmur;
the great ocean flows silently.
That which is deficient makes a sound.
That which is full is indeed peaceful;
the fool is like a half-filled jar,
while the wise man is like a full lake.
Whatever much the ascetic speaks,
it is endowed with meaning and beneficial;
knowing the Dhamma, he teaches it.
He who knows speaks much;
but he who knows and has self-control does not speak much when he knows.
That sage is worthy of silence;
that sage has attained silence.
The Nālaka Sutta, the eleventh.
